utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The next witness is Mr. Knut Vollebaek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation that is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vollebaek.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My first name is Knut, K-n-u-t, and my last name is Vollebaek, V-o-l-l-e-b-a-e-k.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It's the 11th of February, 1946.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, what position do you currently hold?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I am the OSCE High Commissioner on National Minorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And prior to holding this position --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My immediate prior position was Norway's ambassador to the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you briefly set out your previous roles prior to being ambassador to the United States of America.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: When -- where do I start?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: You can begin with your involvement in the foreign ministry 1973, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I joined the Norwegian foreign service in 1973, I have been posted to India, Spain, Zimbabwe, Costa Rica; and from 1989 to 1990 I was state secretary deputy foreign minister in Norway; and from 1997 to March 2000 I was foreign minister of Norway.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, did you testify in the trial of Prosecutor versus Milutinovic in this Tribunal in January 2007?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you had the opportunity to review your testimony in this case recently?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly pause between questions and answers for the sake of the interpreters, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat because I was interrupted and told I that I should pause between the questions and answers so I didn't hear your question, if you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I most certainly will, sir. And just as a reminder, as the interpreter has mentioned, since we are speaking in the same language we need to be mindful about pausing between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I shall pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. Having reviewed your testimony in the Milutinovic et al. case, if you were asked the same questions again, would you provide substantially the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I hope I could have changed the English language but otherwise the substance would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I now seek to tender the Milutinovic transcript which is 65 ter 05200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P01071, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you also testify in the trial of Prosecutor versus Milosevic in this Tribunal in July 2002?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And have you recently had the opportunity to review your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I have looked at that also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And having reviewed your testimony in the Milosevic case, if you were asked the same questions again, would you provide substantially the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I understand there were some misunderstandings with respect to dates that were lately corrected, but otherwise I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I now seek to tender the Milosevic testimony of this witness, and that is 65 ter 02632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That too will be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01072.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And finally, sir, did you provide a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in this Tribunal in January 2002?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And having -- have you had the opportunity to review this statement recently?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And having reviewed the statement, are you satisfied that its contents are true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this witness's statement into evidence and that's 65 ter 02634.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01073.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I will now read out a brief in-court summary of Mr. Vollebaek's evidence, Your Honours. The witness held a number of offices in the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1973 to 2000. From the 1st of June, 1993, to the end of that year he was deputy co-chairman for the International Conference of former Yugoslavia, which dealt with Balkan issues. In that year, in 1999, as the Norwegian foreign minister he also served as the chairman in the office of the OSCE. The witness will describe the OSCE's mandate, origins, and membership. In 1998, the OSCE received a special mandate to deal with Kosovo. The witness will describe impressions of and discussions with Slobodan Milosevic, Nikola Sainovic, Milan Milutinovic, and other officials in relation to Kosovo. The witness will describe his visits to Kosovo that in March 1999 he observed a build-up of Serbian forces. The witness also observed a large number of people travelling on tractors. The numbers were greater than he had seen on previous occasions, and he observed that the situation in Kosovo had worsened. The witness had discussions with Milosevic regarding this build-up of forces and the displacement and burning that he witnessed. The witness met with Ibrahim Rugova several times and observed that Rugova showed a willingness to negotiate with Milosevic. On several occasions, he liaised between Ibrahim Rugova and Slobodan Milosevic. He also met with representatives from the KLA. The witness will testify about his decision to withdraw the OSCE from Kosovo. That's the end of the in-court summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this is my business, but could I make one correction to the summary that I think the representative of the Prosecutor as far as I can see says "in that year," that could lead to a misunderstanding that it refers back to 1993, and it should of course be 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Sir, as you know, your testimonies and your statement are before the Trial Chamber, and therefore I only have some questions that relate to clarifying and highlighting certain areas of your evidence. Now, let's begin with the OSCE, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe. Sir, in your statement at paragraph 5, page 2, you state that you were the chairman-in-office of the OSCE in 1999. That's the same reference in the B/C/S. Now, before we go into the details of your role as chairman, could you provide some background on the OSCE. What is the OSCE and what was its role?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The OSCE is a pan-European security organisation. It was established on the basis of the Helsinki Declaration of 1975. It started as a conference and the organisation itself was established in 1994. The system, if I may say, is that there is a rotating chairmanship which is taken by foreign ministers of each or different participating states. And in 1999 I, as then-Norway's foreign minister, had the chairmanship of the organisation. At that time, if I recall correctly, it was 54 participating states, as we call it, because the legal status of the organisation is a little bit doubtful. Today there are 56. But I -- as far as I recall there were 54 in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned that you were the chairman of the OSCE in 1999. Could you tell us what your responsibilities were as chairman.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The responsibility of the chairman is to -- I may say to run the organisation. There is a Secretary-General that has the administrative responsibility; and the chairman-in-office, as it is called - or now the chairperson in office since we have a female foreign minister as -- chairing it - is more a political role. So it's taking on the priorities, the activities, the direction of the organisation, and trying then, since this is a security organisation, to address security issues that come up within the participating states, conflict prevention, conflict resolution. And in that respect, Kosovo, in my time as chairman-in-office, became of course a very important issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mention in your statement that the OSCE received a special mandate in 1998 concerning Kosovo, and this is in the English page 3, paragraph 4; and in the B/C/S, page 3, paragraph 2. Now, could you explain to us, sir, what the OSCE's special mandate in relation to Kosovo entailed.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The mandate that was given to the OSCE by the Security Council, I think that relates to two Security Council Resolutions, if I remember correctly, 1166 and 1190, I think both are from October 1998, but be that as it may, there were two Security Council Resolutions that asked the OSCE to monitor the situation, to keep the Security Council informed, and then also try to address the conflict in order to find a solution to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you said that in respect to Kosovo in your time as the chairman-in-office of the OSCE, Kosovo was an important issue. Now, could you provide some background on why Kosovo was an important issue at that time for the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as this Court, Your Honours, is very well aware of, this is a major European problem and a major European issue. We were then at -- when I started as chairman-in-office, we were at the brink of a war because it was obvious that the situation between the Kosovo Albanian population of Kosovo, which was then a part of Yugoslavia, and the leadership in Belgrade was -- well, yes, on the brink of war, so to say. It was a conflict that was a very serious conflict. And also we saw a situation where one group of peoples, the then-Kosovo Albanians, were harassed, intimidated, persecuted in a way that was contrary to any kind of standards of human rights and particularly then, of course, contrary to the whole -- whole -- the principles of the OSCE. As you will recall Yugoslavia at that time, because of its policies were -- was already suspended from the organisation. But I had made it clear also to Mr. Milosevic, whom I met already in 1998 in my capacity as foreign minister, that I aimed at bringing Yugoslavia back into the OSCE. I thought that was very important for Europe and also for the situation in that region. And so that's why I took this on as a major task, in order to see if we could bring Yugoslavia back, defuse the tension, and make sure that we didn't have a conflict that would have a spill-over effect also for the whole region.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now I would like to call up 65 ter 00455, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, a document will appear shortly on the screen. Sir, are you able to recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, that's the Security Council Resolution as far as I can see. I can't -- yes, I probably can read it if I can get closer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Would you be able to zoom in a little bit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So is that more visible?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, this says: "Security Council Resolution 1160, 31st of March, 1998. Now, the second paragraph beginning: "Welcoming the decision of the Special Session of the Permanent Council of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe of 11 March 1998 ..." Could you comment on that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If you want me to comment on the decision of the Special Session of the Permanent Council, I don't think I will be able to do that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to provide any background to the reference here without referring to the decision per se?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I guess this must have been a discussion on the situation in Kosovo, but -- because this was before my time as chairman-in-office, we had a Polish foreign minister as chairman, I was part of the Troika, I should probably have known, and if I had been able to go through my papers I would probably know; but if you look at the third paragraph, of course, it refers to the situation in Kosovo, and I suppose also then that a Special Session was dealing with the situation in Kosovo. But I cannot go into detail about what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could move on then to paragraph 7 of this same document. I believe it's in the next page, and if we could zoom in on paragraph 7. Could we zoom in on paragraph 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to see that paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Would you be able to comment on this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as I -- I've already stated, I mean, we have the major efforts to find a peaceful resolution to the crisis in Kosovo, and this then gives us the support of the -- of the Security Council of the United Nations, which we, of course, needed. As you may know, the OSCE doesn't have a mandate as such like the United Nations through its Security Council to take on - what should I say? - conflict resolution. And so we needed a mandate from the United Nations in order to do the activities that we wanted to do in order to find a resolution to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will be Exhibit P01074.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I now call up D160, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's another Security Council Resolution. None of them are from October, I understand, as I said, one from March and the other from September. But this is 1199, the other one that gave the OSCE the mandate to address the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If and we could just move on to paragraph 4 of this resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 4 which is at the top of the page refers to the earlier resolution that we just saw. Would you please comment on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, it -- well, as you see, it says: "Demands further that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in addition to the measures called on under the previous resolution, then implement immediately the following ..." And then you have some concrete measures that should be taken: "Cease all action by security forces ... "Enable an effective continuous international monitoring... "Facilitate, an agreement with the others the safe return of the refugees ..." Which was another important issue. "Make rapid progress on the dialogue between the Albanian community and the authorities in Belgrade ..." So these were the four main activities that I did address as chairman-in-office at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Sir, we've already heard some testimony before this Trial Chamber on the role and function of the Kosovo Verification Mission. Could you tell us, what is the relationship between the OSCE and the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As you will see in this paragraph (b) -- 4(b), it says that we should have an international monitoring or continue the effective international monitoring in Kosovo, and this was done then at the first place through a group called K-D-O-M, KDOM, as far as I recall. And then in -- well, I guess it must have been in October then, 1998, there was an agreement signed between Milosevic and Richard Holbrooke, to which -- and then later on between Foreign Minister Geremek and President Milosevic, to which President Milosevic then accepted the establishment of what we called the Kosovo Verification Mission. And the -- so the Kosovo Verification Mission then was established as an agreement between the OSCE and the Yugoslav president in order then to continue verification in Kosovo and strengthen it -- was the aim -- was to strengthen the monitoring.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And what was your role in relation to the deployment of the Kosovo Verification Mission to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, the deployment started already before I took over as chairman-in-office on the 1st of January, 1999. I think at least some of the members were in place before Christmas of 1998. It was in full force, I think, in February 1999, when I -- during my chairmanship. We -- Norway had a lead role in the -- as a lead nation in the implementation of this agreement, and I was, as far as I could recall, not directly involved in the negotiations but my staff was heavily involved. So Norway was very actively involved in the negotiations for the agreement and the implementation of it also before I took over as chairman-in-office.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we now call up P835, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The last document, it's already an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The number is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I know that there is an -- that there was an agreement. I -- if you hadn't shown it to me, I wouldn't necessarily have recognised it. But, yes, there was such an agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could go to the last page of this document - and this may assist with your recollection. The second-last page. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, at the bottom left-hand corner --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- the name chairman-in-office --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Office --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, "Geremek" appears above chairman-in-office, Mr. Bronislaw Geremek?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Who was Bronislaw Geremek?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Bronislaw Geremek was a foreign minister in Poland and he was my predecessor as chairman-in-office of the OSCE. He was chairman-in-office for the period 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we move on to the first page again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, the paragraph beginning: "The OSCE Kosovo Verification Mission ..." This is below Roman numeral I which is headed "Establishment and Termination" refers to a resolution of the UN Security Council, calling upon the OSCE to establish the mission. Could you explain what this paragraph is referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: This paragraph then refers to Security Council Resolution 1190, as far as I recall, which gave us then the necessary mandate to have a monitoring mission in Kosovo and asked us to implement that resolution, which we then did through this establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd now like to move on to another area. This is the reporting procedure between the KVM and the OSCE. Could you tell us where the OSCE Secretariat was located?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the OSCE was at that time and still is located in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And could you explain to us what the reporting procedure was, if any, in relation to the verifiers on the ground and the OSCE Secretariat in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The Kosovo Verification Mission was one, you may say, even though it was special, but it was one of a number of field missions that the OSCE had at that time and still has today. And these field missions are then requested or are expected to report to Vienna to the Secretary-General, meaning political office of the Secretary-General that will receive these reports. The reporting varies, of course, according to activities and the importance of the situation. As far as I recall, in the situation in Kosovo there were almost -- at least part of the time there would be daily spot reports. I don't know if that was for the whole year, but at least to a large extent there would be daily reports because of the seriousness of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, these daily reports that you mentioned which were then sent up to the political office of the Secretary-General in Vienna, what would happen to them after that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know exactly what happened to them, but they would probably be analysed and they would, I guess -- I don't know if they always would, but at least to -- sometimes if they were important news they would be disseminated, particularly then to the members of the Troika, the leadership of the organisation that is organised through a Troika, which is the previous chairman, the present, and the future. And then based on this, of course, action would be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 00662, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, this document on the screen, are you able to comment on the type of document it is, if you know?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, this would be -- would be a KVM spot report -- or here I see they call it "Interim Report." But it would be one of these daily reports. I see it covers the day of the 10th of January, so I suppose then it means that it's a -- it's just for that day. And it would go through then the different areas of responsibility for the mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we have a look at the second paragraph, the second line, there is a reference to the situation of the eight VJ prisoners being held by the KLA. Was this something you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I -- as far as I recall, I visited Belgrade just the following day. The visit was scheduled in advance because, as I said, Kosovo was such an important issue. Very soon after I took over the position as chairman-in-office, I wanted to go to Belgrade and also then on to Kosovo to discuss the situation. When I planned this visit, I didn't know that this hostage situation would come up, so a lot of time was actually devoted to that in my conversation with Milosevic who was, of course, very upset with it, and also then when I came to Pristina we -- this was followed up and we -- as far as I recall then, we managed to release the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01075.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned this meeting you had with Milosevic in January 1999. Could you give us other examples, if any, of when you met with President Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I met with him on several occasions during my time as foreign minister, I already came to Belgrade in 1998. But during my period as chairman-in-office, as far as I recall, the 11th of January was the first one, but because of the so-called Racak massacre I came back already, if I recall correctly, on the 15th of January. And then I must have been back one more time, I think, in February or early March. So those were my visits to -- probably early March, that were my visits to Belgrade. I spoke with him on then on some other occasions on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this Racak incident that you mentioned - and that's set out in the statement page 5, paragraph 7; and the B/C/S is page 5, paragraph 2 - would this have been an example of an incident that would have been reported via the KVM reporting procedure that we just spoke about?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you explain how information on Racak was reported from the ground level verifiers and upwards?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, Racak was somewhat special. I cannot recall that I had any written information about it because it kind of broke into the -- into the media through the statements made by the head of the Kosovo Verification Mission, Mr. William Walker, which meant that we had to deal with them immediately. So there was maybe some kind of an unusual reporting in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if it were more of a usual incident, for example, if it were violation of the Jovanovic-Geremek Agreement that we just saw, how would that information have been passed on?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, it would have, as we talked about earlier, gone from the mission to the secretariat and then probably some information -- but also then there was a lot, of course, information going on on the phone also between Oslo and Vienna, and Oslo and Kosovo and -- or Pristina, because since this was such an important issue but also a very difficult and dangerous situation. It was important to be more or less continuously updated, which meant that my staff, not myself, but my staff would be on more or less continuous contact with the different parties to the activities, which then was both the secretariat in Vienna, of course, but also then the government in Belgrade and the mission in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, what was your role in relation to the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, my role then was -- or became particularly to try to secure that we could continue having a head of a verification mission, because in view of Mr. Walker's statements, President Milosevic wanted to declare him persona non grata and throw him out, which would have as I saw it -- well, it was a violation of the agreement because I was the one to appoint the head of the mission, and I was to appoint -- the person to sack one; it was not President Milosevic's prerogative. And also it would -- it would ruin the whole mission. I mean, we wouldn't have been able to continue the activities as I saw it. So I went, and urgently, to Belgrade and negotiated with President Milosevic, and after some deliberations I secured his continued presence and position as head of the verification mission.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what about investigations relating to the Racak incident?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That was, of course, very important. We wanted immediately to have investigators and forensic experts. Mr. Milosevic was skeptical or reluctant. As far as I recall, he then said that he would call his own forensic team. And if I remember correctly, he called some forensic team from Belarus, while the OSCE then engaged a Finnish forensic team -- at least there were some Finnish leadership. I don't know if it was composed of others also. But because of the problems we had with President Milosevic at that time and the other forensic team that was already engaged in Racak, it took, as far as I recall, about a week before the OSCE forensic team could get to the scene and to the site and be involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what did they report following their visit to the site?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, there is an extensive report by the OSCE forensic team that I -- I'm afraid I do not recall, but I remember that we had discussions with the leaders of the team, that they were upset or deplored the fact that they had not been able to come to the scene earlier because, as they would probably put it, the evidence was tampered with. And so they had said that they had problems actually verifying what had gone -- had been going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd now like to move on to another area. This is your visits to Kosovo. Now, you referred to your visits to Kosovo in your statement - that's at page 3, paragraph 6, of the English - and you say you visited Kosovo five times in 1999. And that was three times before the NATO bombing. You also described visiting several villages that were totally destroyed in March 1999. Now, if you remember, are you able to name any of these villages that you saw?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid I can't remember many names, but I remember that we -- in March, I suppose it must have been around the 15th of March because it was close to the withdrawal of the Kosovo Verification Mission, which happened then on the night of the 19th. And I remember then I visited Racak because I visited the sites; that I remember. And then we -- as far as I recall, we also went to a village called Podujevo, or a city, that's more maybe a bigger place than just a village. But then we saw smaller villages in the neighbourhood particularly that of Podujevo that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you tell us how they had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well -- well, they were -- some of them was -- most of the houses, you may say, had been blown off the roofs, there had been shelling, there had been fighting, so the houses had been damaged in a war-like situation, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in addition to seeing these houses, did you also observe -- were you able to observe any people?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we spoke with people in the Podujevo, as far as I recall, we went out to the cars on the way and we spoke to some locals there because we were interested in their assessment of the situation and how they also viewed the KVM at that time. And I also -- by the -- one of the military personnel of the KVM, I was taken both to a KLA post and to one post manned by the army, the Yugoslav Army. They wanted to show me or let me meet with the people that they met with on a daily basis because that was part of their work, so to say, both to monitor and to try to defuse the situation, to talk to both sides. And also then to see how close the military people on both sides were located actually. And also then to show the danger to the civilians because they were then to a large extent kept between these fronts which were very close to each other. And we also then saw, of course, people on the roads, as I have referred to in earlier testimonies. I mean, that was the time when we saw people that I would say were fleeing from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you recall, are you able to provide an approximate number of the people you saw?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, that I couldn't. But -- but they were many enough that we clearly noticed them and commented on it, and I referred to them also later on when I spoke to Mr. Milosevic because they made a great impact on me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And what was his response to the information you conveyed to him?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: This -- this information then came at a later stage. This came -- when I spoke to him -- when I mentioned this to him was actually on the 24th of March morning before the NATO bombing started. And to give a little bit of a background, I didn't know that the bombing would start at that time, but since the Rambouillet talks had broken down, I knew that they were imminent. And I had got an agreement with the then-NATO Secretary-General Javier Solano to make a last effort to convince President Milosevic to have a military observation mission because we couldn't only have a civilian one because we couldn't fulfil our mandate with a civilian monitoring mission. And then I had been promised that if I convinced President Milosevic to allow negotiations to re-open for a military presence, the bombing would be postponed. So this was my offer to him, which he refused because he said there were no problems in Kosovo. Then I referred to my visit on the 15th of March where I had then seen people fleeing, and I had seen houses burning, and I had also seen an increased number of Yugoslav Army -- or representatives of the Yugoslav Army or military personnel that was according to then my military advisors in violation of the agreement because the number exceeded what had been agreed. And that he -- I mean, he laughed at me and said that the people travelling were people on picnic and the houses burning were hay burning and the military personnel, they were there in order to defend me, protect me, and that I was watching too much CNN. So I didn't achieve anything unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Now, you also mentioned that you went to Kosovo after the bombing twice.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to recall where you went on any of these trips?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, of course, I went to Pristina because we met with -- well, we had -- then the OSCE returned to Pristina, so we had people there. But also then we met with the local authorities. I also then -- on my first visit, I don't recall the date, but it was soon after the war ended, I went -- made a point of going to the Decani monastery which is, as you may know, a very important Orthodox sanctuary, and I made that a point in order to show that this war and the actions we had taken were not against the Serbs. We were very adamant that Kosovo should also be a place where Serbs could live. And I stayed over night that in order as a -- to whatever extent it had a meaning, an act of solidarity. And I also then visited Pec, which is the headquarters of the Serbian Orthodox church, and areas in that region. And as far as I recall, I also visited Kosovo Polje, where we actually saw some graves, if I recall correctly, about close to 20 people maybe or something, 40, and we actually also there met with an Orthodox bishop or priest that was there and families that were looking for their -- their dead ones. They were watching the graves. I may have visited other cities or villages, but I must admit, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in relation to the places that you recall visiting, are you able to comment on the condition of the buildings that you saw there?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Many places we saw destroyed buildings, not everywhere, but many places. But our comments at that time and what we also heard from some of the Kosovo Albanians that we met when they were fleeing and also upon their return was that these houses -- of course, some of the houses were destroyed by bombing, there is no doubt about that, but many of them were actually destroyed by people on the ground blowing up houses. I am not a military expert, but I had a number of military experts and advisors which could show me the effect of the blowing off of roofs of houses which meant that there had been not a bombing from the outside on the roof but from an explosion inside that blew off the roof, which meant that there had been ground activities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And where did you meet these Kosovo Albanians who were fleeing who gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we met -- the first group we met on the border between Kosovo and Albania, and that must have been -- it was soon after the war started, so it must have been late March or early April -- I think, actually, it must have been already late March, just some days after the war started, because we could also then hear the planes in Kosovo. And they told stories about their conditions and why they had been fleeing. But then when we came back also then we met with those who had already started returning because some people started returning fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And were they able to tell you who it was on the ground who was blowing up these houses?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, of course, according to the Kosovo Albanians these were Serbs, there were no doubt about that -- they had no doubt. I could not verify that, but according to those who were fleeing, that was their story.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you referred earlier on to the breakdown of the Rambouillet talks. Could you provide some background on the Rambouillet talks.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, this was an effort then when -- when the international community in addition to me as chairman-in-office, one saw that this -- the conflict was building up and one was afraid of a war, and also the Security Council Resolution, as far as I recall, also provided for the European Union and others to be involved. And you had a Contact Group of, if I recall correctly, the United States, France, Britain, Italy, and Russia. And they met and -- in order to try to organise some talks between the Yugoslav government and the Kosovo -- or local authorities, KLA particularly I suppose. And -- well, not only KLA because Rugova was there, so it was a broad Kosovo Albanian delegation. And these talks then, as far as I recall, took place in February, started in Rambouillet, went on for a couple of weeks, and then there was a break. There was a draft agreement or preliminary agreement, to which the Serbs, as far as I recall at that time, were fairly positive but the Kosovo Albanians were not. And so there was a recess for about two, three weeks, and then it was reconvened again in Paris itself, not in Rambouillet, and broke down immediately afterwards because then the Serbs had changed their opinion, as had the Kosovo Albanians. So it -- but it meant that there was still no agreement on this draft agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mention a draft agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we call up 65 ter 474.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if you could tell us if you recognise ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document is a book written by a group of authors. This is not an official document, and I don't believe that it can be used as evidence in this case. If there had been a draft document, then it should be located. We shouldn't be doing this by the use of books, particularly since in this case the witness would be required to read the whole book and then comment it. And what he knew about this draft agreement, he already said. Therefore, this is not the original draft of the agreement, and therefore the witness will not be able to recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will watch that and see what use is intended. Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Carry on, please, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, this document on the screen, are you able to recognise it?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, not in this printed version because I don't think I've seen the -- at that time it wasn't printed like this, but I do remember that there was an interim agreement that was present between the two sides and that was -- that had been basis for discussion. And this was how far they came, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I have here a hard copy of the full agreement, if it will assist you to flick through it and confirm that this is the agreement that you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: With Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not certain that it will help me too much. We -- Your Honours, it's a long time ago, so I remember very well, Your Honours, that we discussed this, but I'm afraid I can't remember each and every article of it. But there is no doubt that it is something called the interim agreement for peace and self government in Kosovo. That is for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a signed document that you have there, Mr. Vollebaek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, because I don't think it was ever signed. That was the problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was -- some may have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it a signed document? Not here. I don't think it is signed. You know, Your Honour, the -- as I said, the Serbs were fairly positive at that time, but the Albanians were not very positive. So that was why one took the recess in order to ask the parties to look at it again and see if there were things that they would -- yeah, to find a common ground then for an agreement. Unfortunately, that worked out maybe differently from what the negotiators had hoped for because the -- the Serbian delegation came back then with a number of changes to what we perceived or we thought they had agreed to while in Rambouillet. So I remember that the negotiators were very upset when the groups met again. So -- there was a text that they had been working on and a text that they took with them home, but it was not signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a difficulty, isn't there? The witness doesn't recognise it. It's not something within his present memory. It appears he thinks no more than that to be what it says it is. I think we'll have to wait for some other time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We will deal with it some other time then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, you were talking about the breakdown of the Rambouillet talks and the Paris talks. Just to confirm, was any agreement reached following these talks between the parties?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Following the Rambouillet and the Paris talks?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, because that was the problem. If there had been an agreement, we wouldn't have had a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could I now call up 65 ter 460, please. If we could zoom in on paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, this is another of these daily reports from the Kosovo Verification Mission, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the first sentence describes your meeting with the President Slobodan Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- as disappointing. Now, could you provide some background to this sentence.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, this was in the -- in the -- in the recess period, so to say, after the first part of the talks in Paris, after the Rambouillet and before the Paris talks, where we then was insisting that in order to fulfil the mandate of monitoring and defusing the conflict in Kosovo, there was a need for an international military presence, an armed presence. And the Kosovo Verification Mission was an unarmed presence and they were not able, as I saw it, to fulfil the mandate. And in order, then, to be able to fulfil the mandate, we wanted or needed an armed presence, like United Nations would have in a number of countries and situations when there are conflicts. But President Milosevic refused this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01076.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we call up now 65 ter 461, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: This is another daily report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And could you please comment on the first sentence of this document.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: This was then after my visit to Belgrade, I went to Pristina, as I often did, and met then with the -- with members of the Albanian negotiating team, probably then Mr. Rugova, and some others I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01077.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd now like to move on to another topic, the withdrawal of the KVM, and this is set out in your statement. It's the last paragraph of the English, and in the B/C/S it's page 12 as well and it's paragraph 2. Now, in relation to withdrawing the KVM on the 20th of March, 1999, you say that the decision to withdraw the KVM was yours. Could you tell us why you took this decision?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I took the decision because it was then obvious for me that the KVM didn't have a role any longer to play. It was a difficult decision, and I had prolonged it for a long time because, as you will recall then, the Kosovo Verification Mission was composed of representatives of a number of countries. And while the KVM at the early stages of its -- of the implementation of the mission had a lot of confidence from the local community, as they realised that the mission could not fulfil their expectations, could not defend them, could not protect them from the harassment and intimidation that they suffered, of course they turned against because they were frustrated and they were upset with this. Which also meant -- it meant two things: One was that the -- well, the view of the mission was deteriorating, but also, then, that members of the mission were, again, harassed by the local population. So I had some ministers of foreign affairs indicating to me that we should withdraw because they had problems in their parliaments and with their local constituency, that their young men and women participating in the mission were in danger. And I then convinced them that we -- as long as there was a possibility or a hope for a peaceful settlement, we should be there. And to me then my personal dead-line, so to say, was the talks in Paris. I said to myself and also to those with whom I spoke, that as long as we have ongoing discussions, we should keep the verification mission there because otherwise it would be a gap between the political activities in Paris and the on-the-ground situation, so to say. And that could -- if the situation on the ground deteriorated, it could also have a bad effect on the political negotiations. As the talks broke down, and it was -- the two parties went home and it was obvious that there were no possibility to have, as I saw it, a peaceful settlement, I then felt that I had no option but to take the decision to withdraw -- the withdrawal. Again, based both then on the situation with respect to the safety and security of the members of the KVM, and I was personally responsible for their safety and security; and also then because of the situation of the view or the perception of the OSCE in Kosovo. We have had, as you may recall, in fairly fresh memory, the situation in Srebrenica, and I would not in any case like to have had a similar situation where we -- as then the OSCE in this case would be standing idle watching atrocities going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in general, could you describe how successful the KVM was in fulfilling its mandate, bearing in mind the time-frame from January to March 1999. Was there change in the success? Are you able to comment on how successful the KVM was generally?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: We were obviously not very successful since we ended up in war, so we didn't fulfil the mandate, which was in a peaceful settlement. As I said, I felt when I visited -- the two first visits I made to Kosovo I felt there was a very good atmosphere between the population and the monitors. There was -- when we were travelling in the OSCE cars there were nice signs, people were happy to see us. When I came on my last visit, which I think that must have been around the 15th of March, the situation had changed, it was a negative attitude. People were angry. And so it was obvious, as I said, that there was a frustration, disappointment, with the mission from the local community side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Are you able to provide a specific reason or reasons as to why the situation had changed by March 1999?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, there were, of course, large or great expectations from the Kosovo Albanian side that we would be able to find a peaceful settlement and find a political -- political solution to the problem, which we didn't. And at the same time there was, I think - and maybe more importantly - an experience on the ground that the situation for the local population was deteriorating, meaning that there were an increased number of incidents where the local population then was harassed. And I then said to Mr. Milosevic that that I felt was, at least in part, due to the increased number of military personnel that we had seen in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to move on now to what you saw in the border, and this is set out in your statement - page 13, paragraph 3, of the English; and page 12, paragraph 4 of the B/C/S. You say you were surprised that at the border there was a large number of people expelled and you saw a stream of tractors coming. Now, to begin with, which border were you at?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: This was, as far as I recall then, my first visit to the region after the war had started, and as I recall it must have been late March or very early April, but I think it was late March. That was the border between Kosovo and Albania. We also had a number of refugees in Macedonia, although in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, but that -- and I visited them afterwards, but my first visit was to Albania. Because we knew -- or we heard then from the UNHCR and from Albanian authorities that people were coming out. And -- so I was at the border fairly early in the morning. I had come up from Tirana to -- I'm afraid I cannot recall the name of the border post. And we were looking in to Kosovo and there was a narrow winding road with the largest number of tractors I ever seen in my life. I didn't know that there were so many tractors in the world. And these were people then that had, according to their stories which we heard as they crossed the border, been expelled and forced to leave their homes and properties in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how did you get this information from these people?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I got it from the people themselves. I'm afraid, I speak neither Serbian nor Albanian, but I normally had very good interpreters. So I had interpreters with me, and I could -- most of these people were -- some had been walking, apparently, but most of them were on tractors or hangars of tractors. And it -- there was a process then on the border. So as they were waiting both -- we developed a system where they got a bottle of water immediately and then a loaf of bread next and then the third station was registry because that was very important for us. And while they were waiting then in this line, I could walk up to these people that were waiting and ask, Where are you from? What had happened to you? And who are you? And all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And did you learn who had expelled them?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, according to these people that came, there were Serbs, as they said, and there were some then military, some police, there were different stories. Also then some claim that they had been out walking in the afternoon and when they came home their apartment was occupied by another couple and protected by the police. So there were different, different stories, but they were all unison in their version of the story that they were forced to leave and they had been told that they were not wanted in Kosovo any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And your reference to registering these individuals, that it was important for you, why was that important?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: According to their stories and what we saw, they had no identification documents. And -- so that had been what we were told, that had been taken from them early -- at an early stage. And they -- their tractors did not have number plates. And apparently that were cut off later in the process, but during -- on the road during -- on the way to the border they were also -- they had lost or they were taken away from them. So according, again, to their stories then, they had been -- this had happened in order for them to not be able to return. So for us it was very important then to make sure that we had a proper registry of these people. So we asked everyone to state their name and address and date of birth and number plates of their tractors and all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that, sir. Now, in your statement you also say - this is the last sentence on page 13: "My impression was that when I met the refugees nobody complained about KVM or NATO but it was the Serb forces that were the problem." Now, in the B/C/S that's page 15, paragraph 3. Sir, the sentence that I just read out to you, that nobody complained about KVM or NATO but it was the Serb forces that were the problem, could you explain for us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I mean by that that when -- in connection with the war, there was, of course, a discussion on the effect of the bombing. War is terrible always; bombing is horrible. And there is no doubt that also the war in the bombing did some damage. But I was surprised then that these people, none of them, as I stated that time and as I repeat today, none of them actually blamed NATO or the bombing for their leaving because that, of course, was Mr. Milosevic's story later on, that these people had been fleeing because of the bombs. And I didn't meet anyone that claimed that. But they had a number of stories then about military and civilian and police that had harassed them and had forced them to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, you've already mentioned that you had occasion to meet the refugees at the Albanian border?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Did you meet refugees elsewhere around this time?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Also at the Macedonian or the border between Kosovo and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. The situation there was different because they -- they were in a kind of no man's land and we built a camp for them there and -- but I also met with a number of refugees there. As far as I recall -- yeah, different organisations, but also NATO actually bought -- or built a military camp for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the stories that you heard about the reasons for fleeing, where did you hear them?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I heard them both places. I mean, they were consistent everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I have no further questions for this witness, and I apologise for going over time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. Mr. Djurdjic, is it going to be more efficient for us to have the necessary break now and let you start after the break or can you continue for the next 12 minutes or so?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is better that we have the break now so that I can be more prepared and continue in one go. In any case, I will do as you please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will do that. We must have a half-hour break for the tapes to be rewound now, Mr. Vollebaek, and we will continue at ten minutes to 11.00. A Court Officer will assist you in the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vollebaek, my name is Veljko Djurdjic, Defence team member of the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. With me is Ms. Marie O'Leary, another team member. First of all, I would like to ask you how to address you, whether you'd like to be addressed with your excellency, ambassador, sir, since I'm not completely familiar with the rules and the protocol given the function you now hold.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I am very easy on protocol, so you can call me Mr. Vollebaek or if the Judges allow you could even say "Knut."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the umpteenth time you have provided another testimony before this Court and that one lasted one hour and 15 minutes up to now. I intend to ask you questions that you have not yet been asked or to offer us a deeper insight into some of the things you have been asked before. Ambassador, in 1998, you were the ambassador of the Republic of Norway -- excuse me, the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I was. First of all, I think it's important that Norway's not a republic. The king will be very upset if we didn't correct that. So Norway's a monarchy, a constitutional monarchy, and I was His Majesty's foreign minister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise for this grave mistake. In that capacity, you were appointed a member of the Troika that presided over the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right. The OSCE had decided before I came in, actually, as foreign minister that in 1999 the -- whoever was foreign minister of Norway would be the chairman-in-office of the OSCE. And we had a change in government in 1997, in which I then became minister of foreign affairs; and in that capacity, I joined the Troika of the OSCE as of 1st of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The chairman-in-office of the OSCE at the time was Mr. Geremek, minister of foreign affairs of Poland. Who was the third member in 1998?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: You ask a difficult question. That was -- in 1998 it was whoever had been chairman-in-office before Professor Geremek, it was Denmark, Denmark, the Danish foreign minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about 1999, who was appointed as the third member, since you and Mr. Geremek were still on board?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It's not an appointment. It's an election by all participating states, it's a consensus. Austria took over from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, when you provided your statement in 2002, you pointed out that you had no access to any documents that had to do with the testimony you provided. Did you, in the meantime, review such documents? Did you acquaint yourself between then and now with those documents, and I mean to say your notes?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as you know, I was called back to witness in the case of Mr. Milutinovic. And when I was called back then, I did -- well, first of all I looked at my -- and I was confronted, so to say, with my testimony in the Milosevic case, and I looked at my statements. And I also have looked at some of my notes and I have recently also then spoken to some of my staff members in order to help my memory, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about corrections, let us try immediately and do two corrections. I think that it was recorded in the transcript that you came to Serbia on the 15th of January, 1999. I'm not sure about that date because I think that the first meeting you had in Serbia was on the 11th of January concerning military troops and the second one was on the 21st of January, of the same year. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If you say so, yes, probably, if you've seen reports on that. I thought it was earlier, but -- because I know that I came back very quickly afterwards, I felt it was too quickly, but it could be the 21st. I wouldn't object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And one more date. We have here an exhibit containing the chronology of major events relating to the Kosovo Verification Mission, and as you said today on the 2nd of March, 1999, you paid a visit to Pristina. After that date and until the departure of the KVM - and that was on the 20th of March, 1999 - there is no mention, as far as I could see, of any visit of yours to Pristina, especially not on the 15th of March. I find it impossible for you to have visited Pristina on the 15th of March without that being recorded. Do you agree that this happened before the war?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If you say so -- again, you may probably be right. As I said earlier, this happened ten years ago. I remember some of the events. I remember the impressions it made on me, but I am -- I stand to be corrected when it comes to dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not trying to correct you. I'm just trying to remind you of certain things. Now I'd like to move to the portion of your statement that concerns OSCE. You said that in 195 -- 1998 the OSCE had 54 members and that it grew in 1994 from the European Conference and became an organisation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, what I tried to say was that the establishment of the OSCE is based on this conference on security cooperation Europe which is established on the Helsinki Declaration of 1975. In order, then, to make it more efficient and an organisation, it changed its name and its status in 1994 to an organisation. And then, as far as I recall, in 1999 then when I was chairman-in-office there were 54, we call them participating states since it's not really a membership organisation as such with Yugoslavia suspended. Today, I know there are 56 participating states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, what was the fundamental mode of operation of the OSCE in terms of decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The OSCE is based on consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said that the FRY was suspended at the time. Were there any other rules and regulations governing the internal decision-making within the OSCE or was this the sole rule that you mentioned, the rule of consensus.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A minute ago you said that the decisions were made by consensus. I'm asking you: Were there any other rules and regulations that would amend this rule when it came to decision-making?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There were a number of rules and regulations, but if you mean that the organisation didn't have the right to take a decision because there was one participating state suspended, we -- that was not perceived as the case. So the organisation was definitely perceived as being able to take decisions with the 53 present participating states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In other words, the consensus was not a sine qua non?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, there was a consensus among those who then did participate then and were present, and -- but one state had been suspended and -- but, that didn't stop us from being actively engaged and that was the view of the 53 participating states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So once a certain number of participating countries in the organisation reached an agreement, this is deemed to be a consensus and you just disregard the rest; or do you need a majority to reach a consensus?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, consensus is a consensus, sir. But it had been agreed by the others that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia violated the fundamental principles of the organisation, and as such could not participate at that time. I may also remind you, sir, that the Security Council of the United Nations, of which Russia is a Permanent Member, and all the other members, accepted that the OSCE was a legitimate organisation that had the right to operate, and as such gave us the mandate. So there was no doubt in the international community of the legitimacy of the organisation and its operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that the United Nations shall not interfere with how the OSCE operates. Now, I would like to move to Security Council Resolutions that laid down the terms of reference for the Kosovo mission mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose, can I please have Exhibit P1074.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, if you would be so kind to take a look at this beginning -- or more precisely, paragraph 3 which starts with: "Condemning the use of excessive force ..." Would you be able to comment this particular part of the resolution, your own comment?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, it states -- it states clearly that we -- or the international community at that time condemned any kind of violence that had or did take place in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it says here that the Serbian police forces are being accused of applying excessive force not in -- proportionate --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat. The interpreter didn't understand his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, there was some difficulty experienced by the interpreters following your meaning in your last question. Would you find reformulating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, in this paragraph, an excessive use of force by the Serbian police forces is being condemned against civilians, but also that applies to all terrorist acts undertaken by the Kosovo Liberation Army as well as any support to terrorist activities in Kosovo, including finance, arms, and training.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please move to item 2, if possible. That's on page 2, the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: With respect to this item, I would like to ask you whether you are aware that the leadership of the Kosovo Albanians had condemned terrorist acts?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, sir, you referred to paragraph 2, where it says: "Calls upon the Kosovar Albanian leadership to condemn terrorist action." I know that there was disagreement, as you know, as well as I do, probably better, there were different political parties and factions on the Kosovo Albanian side and there were some that were more - what should I say? - willing to accommodate with President Milosevic and other. Mr. Rugova was one of those who were looking for a compromise, while others did not want such a compromise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question was: After this resolution was passed, did any political party of the Kosovo Albanians condemn these terrorist actions? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could be, but I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We can now see Exhibit Number D160. Ambassador, we are now going to look at Resolution 1199. Would you agree with me that this actually represents a basis and a legal basis, actually, for the introduction of the Kosovo Verification Mission and all the subsequent legal instruments that were adopted at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If it was the basis for all the subsequent legal instruments, I'm not certain, but it was definitely the resolution that we used as a basis for establishing the KVM, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, if we look at item 1 we see that the Security Council is actually requesting a cease-fire to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what we tried to achieve, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in item 2 they demand that the humanitarian situation be improved in order to avoid a humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then in item 3 they call upon the parties to establish a political dialogue in order to seek a solution, a negotiated political solution; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we turn the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vollebaek, as regards item 4, I'd like us to comment sub-item (a). Do you agree that, pursuant to this item, the FRY forces were requested to halt all actions only with respect to the civilian population, and that there is no mention here of any terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I guess that this (a) mentions the security forces, yes, that must be the Yugoslav Army, yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but only with regard to the civilian population but not terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It -- yes, it looks like that's the case, yes. But -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit P835.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us clarify one thing, Ambassador, and I think that it's been there from the beginning of this trial. I may be wrong but you were, at the time, a witness and a participant in those events. In the aftermath of the Resolution 1199, the US launched a diplomatic initiative through Mr. Holbrooke, who held talks with the president of the FRY as a Special Representative; do you remember that? And as far as I know -- just can you say yes for the first part of my question?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, if the first part of the question is whether I remember that there were talks between Ambassador Holbrooke and President Milosevic, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to the evidence in file and some other indicators, we have never heard of any document signed by Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic, but that - if I'm not wrong - the outcome of these talks was an agreement for the Kosovo Verification Mission between Mr. Geremek, the chief office of OSCE, and Mr. Jovanovic, who was the foreign minister of the FRY, and I think that took place on the 16th of October, 1999 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: In one way, sir, if I may say so, I'm to a certain extent happy that you haven't seen the document between Mr. Holbrooke and Mr. Milosevic either because I haven't and I was very upset at that time that I hadn't seen it because it was referred to at numerous occasions by Mr. Milosevic when he disagreed with me. So I was very upset about not having seen it. But that be as it may because we did have a basis for the establishment of the KVM in the agreement that you just referred to, sir, which was a signed agreement between the Government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the OSCE through its chairman-in-office, and I would say that whatever agreement there might have been between Ambassador Holbrooke and President Milosevic then opened the way and prepared a basis for this agreement that we -- that we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
