utterances.text: Thank you. It's been ten years now, or rather, 11 years now. Over this period of time, have you ever seen this Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement or not?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I haven't, and I still feel a little bit stupid by not having that, so as late as yesterday I called my then-Chief of Staff who is now Norway's ambassador to NATO to ask if he had ever seen it and he hadn't. And that, to a certain extent, comforted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think you're wrong. This document doesn't exist, the Holbrooke-Milosevic document.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, then President Milosevic was lying to me on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Everybody's talking about these discussions and they believe that it was translated into this agreement. Now, let's move to the agreement, Mr. Ambassador. I'm talking about the Geremek-Jovanovic Agreement signed on the 16th of October, 1998. Can you please look at paragraph Roman numeral I, item 1. Ambassador, based on this agreement was there any establishment of the Kosovo Verification Mission envisaged?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, we started very quickly. I mean, as you see, it says that we should be able to establish a mission, and we did. And as I said earlier today also, we had people in place already before Christmas of 1999 -- 1998, sorry, sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now look at item 5. Ambassador, do you recall that the KDOM was set up sometime in midyear, or rather, late June/beginning of July, and that it compromised the diplomatic monitoring missions of Great Britain, European Union, USA, France, and I think the Federal Republic of Germany, I'm not sure. And this item provides until your verification mission becomes operational they were going to conduct these affairs?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm afraid, sir, that I cannot confirm the composition of KDOM, but I agree with you that KDOM was established before KVM; and KVM was the successor to KDOM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like now to move to chapter -- Roman numeral II, and that's on the next page. Roman numeral II, item 1. In your view, what was the principal task of the verification process for the mission that had just been established?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we should verify, as it says, in compliance with all parties of the Security Council's Resolution and report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please now look at Roman numeral III, item 1.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I just got the first line, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, you'll get the next page shortly. Am I right in saying that in separate mandate, under 1, one of the tasks is to verify how cease-fire is being maintained.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's certainly so, and I -- the mission also did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under item 2, does it provide for information about the movement of forces in the previous week be handed over or dispatched to the Kosovo Verification Mission?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It says so in the agreement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this: Were you familiar with this agreement in 1998 and 1999 when you were --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Of course I was familiar with --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- chairman-in-office of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That was the basis for my activities. So I wouldn't have done my job if I hadn't familiarised myself with the document, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please now look at item 3.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I already did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see how you understand item 3. Did you have any discussions with Mr. Walker concerning the application of this item 3 of this separate mandate? Were there any issues between the two and did you discuss them? Were you encountering any problems?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then regarding item 2, were there any discussions and problems between the two of you, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection. Of course you will know, sir, that I did not receive all the reports that were sent to KVM. I was not the recipient of all KVM reports to Vienna either. I got the reports that my staff considered it was necessary for me to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Given that we have established that Mr. Walker was at the head of the verification mission and that all decisions in the name of the mission were taken by him and you were the highest-ranking officer in the OSCE who had sent this mission, I'm interested in how this flow of information went between Mr. Walker and you as a political figure. Now, in that respect, would you please look at item 4. Concerning item 4, were you being informed by Mr. Walker about certain problems in terms of their applying or employing the mission on the ground?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I -- I was informed when there were problems, yes, and I was informed, for instance, as I referred to earlier today the question of the Racak massacre, that created a problem between the Government of Yugoslavia and the mission. But I would like to remind you also, sir, that of course there was a leadership team of the KVM mission. You refer to Mr. Walker as a kind of -- the only one. He was definitely the head of the mission, and I of course related to him, since I had appointed him; but when I visited Pristina and visited the mission, we were also sitting together with a whole leadership team where there were a number of different persons from different nations responsible for different parts. So this was a team-work and not a one-person activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. What I told you about is something I learned from the various members of the mission, such as General Javier and Mr. Ciaglinski and Mr. Drewienkiewicz. I was referring to some information they provide during their testimony on the work of the Kosovo Verification Mission and its seat in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P837 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, no. But I may have seen it but I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This should be, or rather, it is the minutes of a meeting. The document was signed by Mr. Nikola Sainovic, Mr. Vlastimir Djordjevic, General Klaus Naumann, and General Wesley Clark. As we will see, it has to do with Resolution 1199 mentioned in paragraph 2 and the position of the federal government, which agreed to its implementation since its official signed it. I just wanted to acquaint you with this page of the document, and perhaps now we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the English version as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, in late 1998 and early 1999, and in the course of that year, were you familiar with this document and its contents?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I cannot recall having seen this document, but I was familiar with an agreement or an understanding between -- well, us, the international community being represented by NATO and the Yugoslav government on the level of numbers of military presence or security equipment -- or security presence in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you about this for the following reason: I was wondering whether there is any reason for me to go through this document if you were not familiar with it and if you were not implementing it at the time.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I cannot judge that, sir; that must be up to you. But I may have seen it but I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try then and go through it briefly. In para 1, under that paragraph in its second part, in its second paragraph, did it envisage for the FRY to take on the obligation of reducing or down-sizing its security presence in terms of personnel in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I was not privy to this negotiations, that was not my task. I had -- first of all, as I recall, this document was already signed in 1998 during the previous chairman-in-office. So it may be that the then-chairman-in-office was more involved than -- in it. So I was only informed at a later stage that there were certain limits to the presence of the -- or to the number of the security forces present in Kosovo and that there were an agreement on that number. And as far as I recall, that was not disputed in my conversations with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next look at item 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I won't go into any other details since I realise that your knowledge of this document is only general, because you had a very senior position in 1998 as well. In any case, am I correct in saying that in item 7 it was envisaged that the withdrawals and deployments of the FRY forces will be terminated by noon on the 29th October, 1998, and at the latest until --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: By noon the 27th of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: -- and at the latest by noon on the 29th of October the KDOM will be notified on the new structures and numbers.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I see that from the exhibit on my screen, sir, but I -- and I cannot recall those dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The dates are not so important. I'm interested in contents. Do you remember that NATO issued an order to attack the FRY which was suspended subsequently, and the FRY was expected to meet the obligations envisaged by the document that we have before us?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I understand your question, sir. This document was dated in 1998, and to my knowledge there was no order by NATO to attack Serbia in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: NATO did issue an order. By virtue of Mr. Solana's decision, it was stayed. All of these agreements had dead-lines that had to be met in that respect. Perhaps you do not recall that NATO Activation Order?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I obviously do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, given what we just saw, and this served as the basis for verification, there were dead-lines set and it was also determined that the KDOM was to notify those in charge on the compliance. Do you remember that the FRY indeed complied of which both the OSCE and the UN were informed?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I do not recall, but -- no, I don't -- but I -- but since we were working on this and there was a process with the implementation of the Security Council Resolution and the implementation of the Kosovo Verification Mission, I -- my understanding was -- or I got information that the basis for the implementation of our activities was in place. So that -- I guess that means that it was by those who should have or should do the verification they were satisfied that we could go ahead with the implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, please have a look at Roman numeral III of this document, its last sentence. That sentence begins with: "However, as a last resort ... the State authorities ..." And so on. Do you agree with me, Ambassador, that the signatories of the agreement agreed that the FRY had the right to respond to terrorist attacks directed against the authorities and citizens in such circumstances in which the lives and safety are jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but if you, by that, imply that the activities taken by the Yugoslav government in Kosovo were proportionate and designed to do that and that we overreacted by withdrawing the KVM and the war, I would refute that, sir, and say that I disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't reached that period yet. We're still at the beginning. We're now merely reading through the agreement. I wanted to know when it was signed and what was signed. We are about to move to the process of verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next have Exhibit P836.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: My first question in this regard is this: Were you familiar at all with this agreement reached in late 1998 and during your mandate in 1999?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, and I don't think I should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. It is one of the documents that the KVM was supposed to implement. In any case, let us move on. Ambassador, did you actively participate in the formation of the verification mission following the decision on its establishment?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not in -- on a daily basis. I took it upon myself to assist the then-Foreign Minister Geremek in the implementation of this agreement, and Norway became a lead nation in the establishment. So I know that my staff was very much actively involved, but I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will not go into any details then, but I wanted to ask you something about the status of the different members of the verification mission on a general level, and I don't mean their international status as diplomats in the FRY but their status within the OSCE itself. Were they international officials within or working for the OSCE as the representatives, or were they the representatives of their states, or both perhaps? Basically, who did the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission work for?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: They, of course, worked for the OSCE and they were responsible to me and to nobody else, as all international civil servants are supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who paid the members of the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, you ask difficult questions. Now, I guess they were -- some came probably from the OSCE budget, but most of it was extra budgetary funds I would think because this was an extremely costly operation, and -- so a number of us paid. I know that Norway paid quite a bit. So I guess one went around begging for funds as international organisations normally do and -- in order to be able to finance it. But to make it clear, the salaries of course to my knowledge came from -- well, came from Vienna, but I have to correct myself there. Maybe we have a system in the OSCE of secondment. So it could be that some of the members were actually seconded. That could very well be. But still, they would be employed by the OSCE and then, in this case, for instance, Mr. Walker by me, appointed by me. But it could be that some of their salaries were -- for some of them were seconded. I don't -- I cannot recall the situation, actually, at that time. Today we have a system where some people are seconded and some are not. In my office, for instance, here in The Hague, I have some seconded people and some that are paid directly by the organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I understand you well -- well, let's try to use the example of the relationship between Norway and the OSCE. Norway, as a state, made payments to the OSCE funds, and then the OSCE made use of those funds as needed?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct. But in addition to this kind of membership fee that we pay into the budget, the OSCE is also heavily dependent upon extra budgetary funds. That means that countries pay to a specific project in addition to what is their membership fee. And I know that in the case of KVM we needed extra budgetary funds in order to make that operation possible because the OSCE didn't have budget that would allow for such a costly and big operation. But in -- and so it is partly then coming from the ordinary budget of the OSCE and partly coming from extra budgetary funds from the different participating states.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to reporting. Was the OSCE and its staff in Pristina duty-bound to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was the KVM and its staff in Pristina duty-bound to report to the OSCE, i.e., to you in Vienna since you were the chairman-in-office?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: They were -- they were reporting to the OSCE, yes. They were not reporting directly to me. They were reporting, as I said earlier, to the secretariat; and then I was informed on a need basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the relevant time, were you informed that reports were being sent outside the OSCE from the Pristina headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I was not, and that would have been a violation of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge of what the criteria used -- what was the criteria used to select those working for the OSCE in terms of their nationality and qualifications?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we, first of all, tried to get the best people possible to meet the requirements of the position that they're going to fulfil; secondly, one is also then looking for a balanced representation from the different areas or different regions of the -- from where the participating states come.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned several times towards the close of your examination-in-chief that this was a civilian verification mission not a military one, and that in your view it should have been a military one. Don't you think that a civilian mission has greater weight than a military mission or a military presence in a given territory would have, particularly since it had to rely on its civilian verifiers representing the international community?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that I said that I wanted the KVM as such to become a military mission, but I wanted it to change its position in February when it became obvious that President Milosevic didn't respect the agreement and the mandate of the mission, and the mission, being a civilian mission, could not fulfil its mandate. I agree with you that there are many -- many advantages to a civilian mission, but that, of course, requires that both sides comply with it. It doesn't have a cloud. It doesn't have -- it doesn't have power to implement its mandate if the two sides or whatever sides you have don't cooperate with the mission. And we saw then that the sides, also the KLA, did not respect the mission. So we, of course, had to address that on several occasions also. But -- so we lost power. We couldn't fulfil the mandate, and in that way, I could not accept to have a mission continuing without fulfilling its mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, according to the agreements and the resolution we saw, the basic and primary task of the verification mission was to monitor the cease-fire and eventual violations of it. Having in mind the way the mission worked and implemented that, it started being very efficient as of January in that regard. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I -- as I said earlier, I felt that when I visited the -- Kosovo, particularly maybe the second time -- you know, when I came at the first time, it was at the beginning of its mission and they had not deployed everywhere. So I got the impression at that time that maybe they were not in full force yet. But then when I came there the second time, I felt it was fairly efficient, it was well received. And then when I came back the third time, and that may have been the 2nd of March as you say -- I'm sorry that it was that early because it proved then that the agreement that we had really were undermined very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. I will try to jog your memory a bit since we are on that topic. You were in Belgrade for the first time to attend the talks with the FRY president on the 11th of January, 1999. Unfortunately, no substantial matters were discussed at that point in time. What was discussed heavily at that point in time were the kidnappings that were occurring in Kosovo at the time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The second time there were any talks in Belgrade was on the 20th of January, 1999, when the FRY government decided to proclaim Mr. Walker persona non grata, and it was because of that that you arrived in Belgrade to express your disagreement, stating that this was meddling with the OSCE policy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Sir, I think it was more than expressing my disagreement. I was telling President Milosevic that he was violating an agreement and that it was none of his business, actually, to withdraw the head of the KVM; that was only by business. And also explain to him that the whole mission would fall. It was not just changing the head of a mission. So -- but that's true, we -- that was the main issue at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to remind you about the dates, and I may have gone a bit more widely. But do you agree that it all had to do with Racak basically?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Certainly. No, the visit on the 20th of January, as you say, was because of Racak and the serious situation then that happened with the -- or occurred or resulted in the -- President Milosevic's desire to declare Mr. Walker persona non grata.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that you said that at that time, irrespective of the Racak problem that we will discuss separately, that the situation was otherwise satisfactory and that people trusted the KVM as well as that it was successfully implementing its mandate, that was in late January 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the situation was satisfactory and that we were fully implementing; I think that is to go too far. But it's true that the -- there were confidence in us from the local population and that we -- that we felt that we could do -- or else I was told and I saw for myself also that there was a good relationship and that we could do the job that we were supposed to do. That doesn't mean that they were not reporting along the way about skirmishes and disagreements and problems on -- with both sides, but we felt that we did a useful job, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you mentioned a rather unusual way that Mr. Walker informed about Racak regarding yourself. You said that you learned about that actually from the newspapers. Am I correct in concluding that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As far as I recall, yes, it was -- anyway, as you say, an unusual way of information. I -- this broke through the media, and as far as I recall, I also learned it through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, don't you think that you, as a chairman-in-office, when talking about this event which has been characterised by many, including yourself, as a massacre, a report should have first been sent to you urgently; and then as a political head or political leader of the OSCE to take a stand on that, instead of Mr. Walker, chief of the staff in Pristina, doing that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. And I told Mr. Walker that very clearly, that I was not very happy with this incident or the way that he handled it. And I also told Mr. Milosevic, because he, of course, wanted to use this for whatever it was worth and even quite a bit more as I saw it, that was right. But at the same time, the mishandling of a report system cannot defend or diminish the gravity of what happened in Racak. And it was, of course, irrelevant for whatever happened. There are two different questions there of totally different proportions. And so it didn't excuse what happened, nor President Milosevic's reaction to it, nor his denial of the forensic mission that the OSCE wanted to send; rather to the contrary, at least in my mind. It strengthened my suspicion that something really wrong had gone on since Mr. Milosevic would not allow the OSCE forensic team to come to the scene immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you this: On what day did you find out about the Racak incident; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, allow me to remind you. The incident in Racak took place on the 15th of January, 1999. Mr. Walker was in Racak on the 16th of January, 1999, and held a press conference in Pristina on that same day. You yourself learned about this from the media, so that could have been the 16th, on the evening, or the next day, on the 17th, if this story was covered by the media?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, if it is correct what you say, that Mr. Walker had a press conference on the 16th, I suppose I would have been informed about it on the 16th; it would have been strange otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you had a contact with Mr. Milosevic after this event?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I do not recall, but I know that I was on the phone, maybe not with Mr. Milosevic, but with the Foreign Minister Jovanovic very soon because this became then a problem. And as a result of that, I went as quickly as possible to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A short while ago you told us that you talked to Mr. Milosevic about the OSCE forensic team. So I would like to know, When was it that you discussed this particular subject with Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I discussed it, I remember very clearly when we had this meeting where we also discussed the situation with Walker, but then it was already clear that the OSCE forensic team had not been allowed in. Again, the establishment of a forensic team is not my business. This is, of course, the organisation's business. And as I said, I spoke to Foreign Minister Jovanovic and I also called Mr. Milosevic on the phone, but if this was then the 17th or the 18th or the 19th, I am not able to recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know at all whether the OSCE team ever arrived in Pristina; and if it did, on which date?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the date, sir, but my -- at least I have seen a report from an OSCE forensic team under, as far as I recall, a Finnish leadership. And I think I even, if I recall correctly, spoke to the person at that time. So I suppose they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that document later. On the 21st January, 1999, Ambassador, you attended talks in Belgrade. According to the report that we are going to see now, I believe that the forensic team on that day was already in Pristina and was working together with the team who had already started work there. Did you know anything about this at that time or even today?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It could very well be. I know that they worked together with the Belarus team, that there was a contact. I don't know when they started working or when they finished working, but I know the Finns were -- or the head of the team who was a Finn and, as I said, was dissatisfied and regretted that they could not have been there earlier. And they claim that the report was not as good as it could have been if they had been on the scene earlier and without having this team from Belarus arriving at an earlier stage and being active there before they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Mr. Walker was in Racak on the 16th January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, he had been to Racak and he had seen -- that was, of course, the whole -- the reason why he had a press conference because he was shocked and he was -- he was very moved. And that was also what I explained to Mr. Milosevic when I saw him then on the 20th, that -- I mean, whatever you say about reporting procedures, I would say that Mr. Walker's reaction to a certain extent was a very sane one, a normal one, from any human being that is witnessing something like what had happened in Racak. At the same time, you might expect that from head of a mission and a seasoned ambassador that there are -- that you control your reactions. But I -- and, again, to a certain extent I have great sympathy for Mr. Walker in spite of the fact that I -- this -- criticised him for the way he had handled it. But I understand his reaction, so I -- I think it was a normal reaction from his side, in spite of the fact that it may not have been very helpful at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to some estimates, he headed off towards Racak on the 16th of January, accompanied by 50 journalists and TV crews altogether, and that is when he left Pristina. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I didn't know the number of TV crews or anything like that, but I suppose he was accompanied by some people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Walker inform you that the KLA were in Racak on the 16th of January and that he talked to the commander of the KLA for the Racak zone?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I cannot recall that, but he may very well have done that, but I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember being informed that as early as on the afternoon of the 15th of January Racak was in the hands of the KLA, that they had control over it?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but visiting Racak later -- and as I mentioned earlier today, I saw that there was no problems, seeing that there had been fighting, so there was obviously fighting that had been going on in that area. But I'm not now able to testify to any dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, were you informed that during the visit to Racak on the 16th of January, bodies were removed -- moved around, that casings were picked up as souvenirs, and that the crime scene was not secured, which resulted in its being polluted?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I was informed, as far as I recall, that the crime scene was not secured but I was not informed about any of the other details that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you informed as to when was it the first time that the police forces of Republic of Serbia entered Racak and when the crime scene investigation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could be, but I cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have Defence Exhibit D003-0947 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would just like to inform you about one single fact, and that is that the scene-of-crime investigation report was compiled by the investigating judge of the court in Pristina on the 18th of January, 1999. Now I would like to ask you if you knew that Mr. Gil Gilberson and Ed Soleven from the OSCE were present at the scene?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I cannot recall that I have been informed about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we do not have a translation of this report, but it would assist us if we are provided with a description of this document. I'm not sure if the information provided in the question suffices to inform us of what this document is. So perhaps Defence counsel could tell us at the very least what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First, Mr. Djurdjic, is there a translation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does exist, Your Honours, only I wasn't aware of that. And it's D003-0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the last four digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D004-0035.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to be on the screen now, Ms. Gopalan. That should meet your needs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to emphasize that I'm using this document to put the questions. I am aware that the ambassador is not familiar with this document. I only wanted to know whether he know that two OSCE members, Mr. Ed Soleven and Mr. Fantini [as written] Giovanni were present in the course of the on-site investigation in Racak on the 18th of January, 1999, which is to say, on the fourth day after the event.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As I said, sir, I do not recall. But it wouldn't surprise me, so to say -- I mean, this was, of course, a very important event and I would expect the KVM to follow this up very actively.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador, but as I understand, the KVM made all efforts in order to inform you about everything that was going on and then four days after the event, the Serbian authorities entered Racak. Did they inform you why that happened that way?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could very well be but, sir, again these are actually some years ago and I do not recall every sequence of this. I recall very well when the news broke. I recall my conversations and negotiations with Mr. Milosevic. I recall my later visit to Racak. All that made a great impression on me. Every single detail of what happened in between, despite of the fact that it was serious and important, I do not recall because there were other people between me and the actual implementers that dealt with those on a day-to-day basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I fully understand that, but I perceive you as man number one in the OSCE at the time. Let me ask you one more thing: Had you ever been informed that the KLA had imposed, or rather, requested a precondition that the Serbian investigating judge should be allowed to enter the scene without any security guards except in the presence and accompaniment of OSCE representatives?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could very well be, sir, but I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you had received information about the presence of the KLA in Racak and that fighting had been going on?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As I said, when I visited Racak later on there was no doubt that there had been fighting going on. At what time I was informed about that fighting, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive a report from the verifiers that the Serbian forces had reported to the Kosovo Verification Mission that an operation against terrorist forces was going to be launched in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive a report that former members of the Kosovo Diplomatic Mission from the United States were supposed to be at a certain place in Racak on the 15th of January and to observe the action that was to be taken against the Kosovo Liberation Army and they, however, did not fulfil that task?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I was not and I didn't even know that Kosovo had a diplomatic mission at that time nor in the United States nor anywhere else. It was not an independent state as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Apparently there was a mistake. The Kosovo Diplomatic Mission of the US.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, the United States did not have a diplomatic mission in Kosovo either. I guess they may have had some representatives covering Kosovo from Belgrade, but, as you know, we were all accredited to Belgrade and covered Kosovo from Belgrade and we travelled back and forth. So I guess the only diplomatic mission that the United States had in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in Belgrade, but they might have had people looking after the situation in Kosovo, which we otherwise did at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the 15th of January when these people became members of the Kosovo Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Ambassador, what I have just put to you is a statement of one of the verifiers from the KVM. I wanted to ask you this: Are you sure that you received accurate and true information about any situation in general and the situation in Racak in particular?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fairly certain -- because, you know, we were not only dependent upon the information from one source, our information and the information I received came from different sources. And when we assessed the overall situation with respect to what had happened in Racak, I think the sources that I could rely upon and the information that I received indicated that there had been an action or that had taken place that was a clear violation of basic human rights and that it was actually carried out by military forces against civilians. I understand, for instance, that there were found elderly people in the grave and there were found very young, almost children, and so there were not to my understanding -- and there were no -- I was told there were no military uniforms or anything like that on the people. So it was not -- it could not be put as a result of a military action between two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, this very same verifier told us, or rather, stated in his statement that the FRY army was not in Racak. But let me ask you something different. Did the report that you saw contain the details of the victims as to their gender, sex, age, et cetera? Did you see any details of that kind?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It's, again, difficult to remember, but I remember, as I just said, that I was told that the -- or the information I received indicated at least that the group was not a typical military group. And so I was told about the age of the people and also about the sex of some of them. So -- but exactly how old they were and how many there were under each gender, I was not -- well, I may have been told, but I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was only one female aged, I believe, 19, perished in this incident, and I think she's been buried at the cemetery of the KLA. And there was one young boy, 15 to 16 years of age. All the rest of them were adult males. Has anyone ever told you this what I just told you, or did you possibly have this information at the time?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I had the impression -- I don't recall the number of females and males. I remember -- I was told that there were -- may have been just one female then. I also was told that there was a young boy. But I also was told that there were elderly men that one was -- didn't think would be in any kind of military service. But the number and the age, I may have been told, but I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now you have put me into a very uncomfortable situation. What do you mean when you say "elderly" people? Please, where do you draw the line when you say this person is fit for military service age-wise?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I can assure you, sir, that that line has changed considerably over the years. So the elderly become older and older according to me. But -- so I can't remember exactly at that time 11 years ago I -- probably the line was somewhat lower than what it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. We still have a little time before the break, so I'll ask you about Racak. Tell me, how come that Mr. Walker decided on his own, without your consent, to hold this press conference and to provide the information that he did? So he didn't obtain prior consent from you as the chairman-in-office of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I guess you have to ask Mr. Walker about that to get the real answer. What he told me and what I accepted and understand was that he was so outraged about what he saw and he was so upset that he -- he could not wait, so to say, to make this known. He felt that this was very important. So it was, as he explained it, a human reaction to something that he found was outrageous.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, do you know that trenches had been dug around Racak, that there were fortifications there of military type? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could be, but I must admit that I don't recall that now, but there -- I don't know. I don't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that General Maisonneuve and General Drewienkiewicz was photographed -- the whole area of Racak was photographed on the 16th. Have you ever seen this footage of Racak?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I saw some pictures, yes. Whether those are the pictures you refer to, I don't know, but I saw some pictures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Djurdjic? We will have the second break now, and we will resume at five minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just -- I hope the representative of the Defence knows that I have only today. I'm afraid I can't make many more days available, so that you may inform him that he has to put the important questions to me during the course of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know that was done yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will finish at 1.45 today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that, of course, will allow some time to Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm so sorry to hear that you have to leave because I need to speed things up, but let's finish with the topic of Racak. Were you informed by anyone that the KVM representatives, Mr. Henry and Mr. Pedersen were present when the bodies were exhumed and once the autopsies were under way?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I remember the name Mr. Pedersen. That could be, but I -- again, I must admit that I do not recall. You know, to repeat myself, I was not informed about all the details with this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were informed by Ms. Helena Ranta who was the head of the forensic team from Finland. Did you know that she said that there were no signs of mutilation on the bodies?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember what she said, but what I remember from the report was that they regretted that they had come in late and that there were -- they had problems in part of the verification because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I absolutely agree because one needs certain other elements in addition to the autopsy to have a complete expertise. Did you know that the bodies were transferred from the location to a mosque and the investigating judge found the bodies in that mosque and that subsequently the corpses were transferred to the Forensic Institute?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm not certain about the mosque. I heard that the bodies were transferred, if they were, to this Forensic Institute, whether that was via a mosque or not, I am not able to confirm that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one brief question: Did you know that Mr. Walker threw a pencil at Ms. Helena Ranta during their conversations when he found -- when he saw the findings of the forensic team?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That he threw a pencil at her? No, I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that he exercised pressure as well as the Finnish foreign minister exercised pressure on her in order to change the findings of her forensic team?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I was not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the book she wrote concerning Racak and the work of the team? It goes a few years back.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Ambassador, am I right in saying that the Yugoslav delegation in Rambouillet accepted the agreement that was tabled by the Contact Group?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The first -- the draft agreement that we saw earlier, that I was shown earlier, that was tabled on the 20 -- or that we had then discussions on February -- I guess it was dated the 23rd of February. That -- to my knowledge, that was accepted or not accepted, but it was positively received by the delegation. As you will know, I was not part of the Contact Group, so I didn't participate in the day-to-day negotiations. I was called in twice, once then in Rambouillet and once later on in Paris, to sit with the members of the Contact Group and the two delegations. But when it was decided then to have this recess, my understanding was that the Yugoslav delegation was fairly positive to the draft, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the talks were interrupted because the members of the Kosovo delegation belonging to the KLA had to consult with the commanders in the field first before signing the agreement in Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Whether they wanted to consult with the commanders in the field or not, I don't know exactly, but they wanted to have consultations, yes. But my understanding was also that the Serb or the Yugoslav delegation needed to confirm or to have an approval that they -- I'm not certain that they have the full mandate to sign there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. You know very well that any agreement that is originally signed subsequently needs to be ratified by the state assembly. In any case, let us move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D157 next.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, we will see a KVM report of the 26th of February for the period until the 4th of March, 1999. The first page, the first two paragraphs under the heading "KLA," were you informed about the fact that in the Djeneral Jankovic area a hundred KLA members crossed the border, entering it?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, probably -- I don't know. I can't remember if there were a hundred and all that, but I was informed about different violations, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have a look at bullet point 1. Were you -- did you know that they were actually supporting a mass movement of refugees so as to have that portrayed as one of the consequences of the Serb offensive?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I -- well, I was informed about violations. As I said, if I was in detail informed about exactly what was going on, I'm not certain. And as I said earlier, I was not actually privy to all these reports because they went to Vienna. But there is no doubt that there were violations on both sides, and we opposed both sides in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but I believe this is an important point. The KLA first acted and then manipulated the internal displaced persons so as to paint a picture of a humanitarian catastrophe and to persuade the international community that the FRY were in violation of the agreement, hence providing an excuse for the international forces to intervene. In my view, that is very important.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, they were not very successful then because according to this report we knew what they were doing. So that was not any reason for any kind of international intervention because they were -- this is -- as you told me, this is a KVM report and it clearly says that there is manipulation by the KLA. So if the KLA wanted to manipulate us, they were unsuccessful in manipulating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I think they were successful because on the 1st or 2nd of March, when you arrived in Kosovo, that the situation had deteriorated significantly, that you saw many IDPs, and that you believed that the KVM was no longer able to fulfil its mandate?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, sir, with all due respect, even though this may have been the case, and I don't doubt that because I say we knew there were breaches of the agreement on both sides, we -- I mean, I had with me experts and people from the mission that actually could distinguish who was doing what at what time and where, so we were not that easily fooled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. But the world media carried the information they received from Albanian sources, and that is how the world public opinion was being created.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I did not base my decisions on public opinion, sir, and you will know that the world media misinforms us every day, so that's nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the staff of the KVM as one of the sources of information used the media, i.e., the people working for the various media?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Of course we used media as a source of information in Kosovo, but we also, as you will know, as long as we managed with -- as long as we could have people out in the field, we had field representatives. That's the strength of the OSCE. That's the situation even in Kosovo today. So it means that we have people in the local villages that can inform us directly, so we're not dependent upon second-hand sources for our information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2, please. There should be something saying: "On other locations ..." Can we go back to page 1 in the English version, the first page, please. The second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The part that reads: "On other locations the KLA forces in the Podujevo area managed to carry out an attack in the town itself - effectively taking the fight to the Serbs ..." Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, sir, where are you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, the heading is actually "Elsewhere."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, it was precisely at the time of your visit in Pristina and when you were taken to Podujevo. At that time, the KLA liberated the city, the town, from their point of view, of course. Did you know that at the time when you were in Pristina on the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I think even on the 2nd of March I went to Podujevo, as far as I recall, and I think that the reason why we went there was they had been -- that the KVM had been very actively involved there. And also that this was the time, as far as I recall, that we also saw the KLA position and the VJ position. So I visited both sides and we were told about the military activities in that area as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Such activities in which the KLA attacked and took over Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not certain that I understand your question, whether I was informed about KLA activities; is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just read the part in which it is stated that the KLA managed to enter Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yeah -- well, yes, I -- again, I know that we visited Podujevo because -- because that was an important area for the KVM and they wanted to show me that area and the activities. What I was told, with all due respect, ten years ago or even more than ten years ago, I must admit, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And it is then that you saw the destroyed roofs of houses?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, then and on later occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the part titled "Assessment" and then what follows. Am I right in saying that the subheading is: "KLA: Exploiting the media." And that from this KVM report it is clear that: "... ethnic Albanians will continue to work on international sympathy for their cause. The plight of the IDPs remain their strongest weapon ..." Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose I was. I can't remember that sentence, but we were, of course, very well informed that KLA used the situation for their cause and this was also one of my arguments when I spoke to President Milosevic, that he should be cooperating with us because I couldn't see that he had anything to lose from working with us and accepting our cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at the last sentence in this conclusion: "The KLA are unlikely to wish to provoke another Racak. Therefore, the provocations will be in areas they are confident of either defending or at least free of retribution." Were you informed of that, that is to say that there was information available to the effect that Racak was a provocation to be exploited with the media?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I may have been told about this report. I don't recall that. But even if there was a provocation, which I think happened quite often from the KLA side, I think a proper army or a proper police force, like the Yugoslav Army and the Yugoslav police cannot use provocation as an excuse for attack on civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. When the KLA does that and when they say it was done by the FRY forces, it seems that, again, it was upon the FRY to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any case, could we please move on to P847, item 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, this is a KVM report of the 15th of March, 1999. Please look at item 4, sub-item (a). Did you know that after the KLA entered the area of Kacanik the KLA commander prohibited the UNHCR to evacuate the IDPs there and the KVM interpreted that as an attempt to use the Albanian civilians as a live shield, human shield?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If I was particularly informed about this incident, I am not certain but that could very well be. I was briefed on a daily basis on the deterioration of the situation. And as I said earlier, this was a deterioration that was caused by a lack of -- lack of cooperation with us from both sides. But we were there partly to monitor the situation but also partly to protect the civilians. And because of this lack of cooperation, we could not protect the civilians and the whole reason for our withdrawal was that we could not fulfil our mandate. So this only underlines my decision to withdraw. And also, if you allow me, sir, this was one of my arguments when I had my conversation and discussions with President Milosevic. Why couldn't he cooperate with us? If the culprits were KLA, if the culprits were on the other side and the perpetrators, then of course it could be in his interest to open up the Kosovo region to an international military observer force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I not right in saying that it was in the interests of the KLA to have the situation destabilised in order for international forces to enter Kosovo? That was their goal in view of their ultimate goal of having an independent Kosovo, since having a foreign military presence there would basically be a statement to the effect that this was no longer territory of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: But if, with all due respect, President Milosevic did not [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "not"] want an independent Kosovo, it should have been definitely in his interests to cooperate with us in order to have the international force there because then we could have avoided the war and we could have also, I think, avoided an independent Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I don't want to go into politics. I'd like to stay with the facts during that time. Conclusions are then left to the Court. I especially want to steer clear of any political conclusions. The situation on the 1st of March was destabilised. You see from the documents I showed you that the KLA wanted to provoke a destabilisation. To corroborate that, I would like to move to P1076 and this will have to do with your response having to do with the military presence.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: But, please, if you allow me, sir, one comment before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I will be very brief, but you -- with all due respect, you speak to politician -- I was a politician at that time. I'm not a politician any longer. So my -- I was not a monitor. My task was to find a political solution to this conflict, and, of course, I used political arguments in my conversation with Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree with that. You were the most prominent political figure at the time in Europe. Ultimately it was you who decided to withdraw the KVM. Let's look at this document of the 1st of March, 1999, when you were in Belgrade. In item 2, have a look of what the KVM report was on the results of your visit to Belgrade. Ambassador, am I right in saying that you insisted on NATO forces entering Serbia in your discussions with Milosevic at least according to this KVM report, NATO, military forces, that is to say?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I insisted on -- I don't think it says NATO -- well, deployment of NATO-led military force. That was what we wanted. Yes, that is true. Of course I insisted on that because that was the only solution we saw to avoiding a war. And I explained to Mr. Milosevic that it would be upon his invitation and it would be a situation which was similar to other countries where you have an international military presence. So it would not be any kind of undermining his authority or anything like that, but it would be assisting him in keeping law and order and in avoiding the conflict that we saw looming.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Why NATO forces? Why didn't you turn to the UN so that it could define the mandate of these international military forces? You insisted on the NATO forces. To cut things brief, Norway was at the time a member of the NATO Pact and it was implementing both NATO policies and OSCE policy?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, I think I managed to keep the two hats separately. I was very consistent and concerned that I should be the OSCE chairman-in-office when I -- when I acted as the OSCE chairman-in-office and not the foreign minister of a NATO country. It is quite right that Norway is a member of NATO. At that time, and even today, you will know that the United Nations do not have capacity to be very actively involved militarily, and it was agreed that the most likely and the only realistic military force available on short notice - and we needed a force on short notice - would be NATO forces. So this was not undermining the United Nations. You would also remember that both the chairman of the national -- of the Assembly of the United Nations and also the Secretary-General referred to this as a viable solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Doesn't it strike you as cynical -- well, on the 24th when you had a telephone conversation you said, Invite NATO forces and then we will not bomb you, then that would constitute a voluntary invitation so as to prevent the war from taking place?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, sir. With all due respect, I did not find that cynical at all. I found it a moral obligation. Mr. Milosevic had over the years -- and even harassed, intimidated, misused his power against a people in Europe. We could not, as European states, watch this going on without losing our -- any kind of moral authority. So we were forced by Mr. Milosevic's lack of willingness to cooperate with us to do what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who decided that the FRY should be attacked?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, that -- well, first of all, there were discussion in the -- what you would call the international community because there was a discussion in the United Nations about this. We did not reach, as you will know, a Security Council Resolution on that, which I do regret. I think there should have been a proper UN mandate for this. We did not reach that. At the same time, there were what we call Chapter 7 language in the UN both and by the Secretary-General and the Chairman of the Assembly of the United Nations, which in my view gave the necessary basis for the -- to start the war. And the reason for that was that we were afraid that this could spread to the region. This was not any longer just an internal Yugoslav matter; it was a matter of regional dimension, which then gives, according to the UN Charter, the right of the international community to intervene. So it was an intervention based on the fear of a major catastrophe for the whole region.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, that was a very comprehensive answer. If I understand correctly, it was not the UN that decided the -- that the FRY be attacked. They actually opposed it. So who was it precisely who decided that the FRY be attacked?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The decision to go to war was, as you very well know, sir, taken by NATO. But I would not say, when you have the statements by the Secretary-General of the United Nations and the Chairman of the Assembly, I would not say that the United Nations was opposed. As you know, there were different views and Russia is a permanent -- and China are Permanent Members of the Security Council and they can lay down vetoes. And it was not possible to get a Security Council Resolution for this. But to say that the UN, as such, was opposed, I would beg to disagree with you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Contrary to the UN Charter - I don't mean you, but rather NATO - decided to launch an attack on the FRY; am I right? Just yes or no so that we can move on.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. So you worked in compliance with international law. Let's move on. Did Mr. Walker used to inform you about his meetings with some international figures such as the Chief of Staff of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but I suppose he had meetings with a number of actors on the ground and should; that was why he was there. He had meetings with the representatives of the federal Yugoslav government and, of course, local authorities and KLA. It was part of his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking about officials outside the FRY, representatives of Russia and other countries. So that which went beyond the mission's mandate in the FRY?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That he had meetings with the Russia government; is that what you are meaning? Yeah, well -- no, not -- well, that could be. I must admit, I don't recall with whom he had meetings. He might have had a number of meetings. He was of course an interesting person at that time and we had a number of delegations coming to Kosovo, governmental delegations, and there would probably be governmental representatives from a number of countries. So I wouldn't be surprised if he also met with Russian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he inform you about his meeting with General Ivashov who, at that time, I believe was at the head of the political department of the Russian Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not that I recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember at all that there were objections raised by Russian officials concerning the way in which the KVM wrote its report and also that Mr. Walker was liaising and maintaining contacts with members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not particularly links with KLA. That -- I can't remember that I heard that. I had discussions and meetings with then-Foreign Minister Igor Ivanov, the Russian foreign minister, where he complained about Walker, yes, and he was dissatisfied with the way he was running the mission. And we had discussions with that which I then took up also with Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the KVM left Kosovo and Metohija on the 20th of March and the war started, they did have liaison officers for NATO; right?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There were maybe some liaison officers for NATO in the KVM, I don't know, but that -- yes, I guess -- well, I must admit, I don't recall exactly that but that would not be so surprising maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And do you know what was their assignment? I'm talking about these liaison officers who liaised between the KVM and NATO?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I suppose their assignment was what any liaison officer's assignment is, to keep links open between one organisation and another.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KVM liaison officers used to hand over information received from the KLA to NATO for the purpose of prosecuting a war against the FRY?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I'm not informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know people -- a man called Richard Ciaglinski and David Meyer from the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I can't recall those names, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard that a letter from the KLA was dispatched and sent to General Clark from the Main Staff of the KLA through the liaison officer at the KVM?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ambassador, do you know that during the war, members of the KVM used to go back to their respective home countries and hold press conferences there?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I was not -- I suppose that they would go home to their home countries from time to time, but I was not informed about press conferences that I can recall anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever allow anyone in your country to hold a conference -- press conference during the war in your capacity of the chairman-in-office?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Anyone from the KVM to come and hold a press conference in Norway? Well, as foreign minister you like to hold the press conferences yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You didn't understand me, Ambassador. Did you allow any member of the KVM to go back to their home country, Great Britain, Germany, et cetera, and hold a press conference there in their Ministry of Defence or whatever? Do you know of any such case?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I don't know that I gave that permission ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now read certain portions from a press conference, and I would like you to tell me whether you are familiar with that at all. "As you know, 12 days ago we were ordered to leave. Up until then we maintained contact with the KLA. The air-strikes have positive effects on the ground. The attack launched by the Serbs two days ago near Malisevo has been seriously hampered by air-strikes because four tanks and one artillery placement were destroyed ..." Did you have any of this information at your disposal while you held your position as a chairman-in-office?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I understand what you refer to, sir, but if you say "12 days ago we were ordered to leave ..." of course then this was not during the KVM presence and activity this was afterwards. So I don't know exactly when people were released of their duty. But I would say it's quite different if you hold a press conference after you have left mission or while you are on mission, so I think your argument, with all due respect -- well, I don't understand it. But, yeah -- I don't understand it is my short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, you have understood perfectly. These are speaking notes of Mr. Drewienkiewicz for his press conference in the Ministry of Defence in London, either on the 31st of March or the 1st of April, 1992 -- 1999. Thank you very much for answering my questions, and I'm very sorry that I had to shorten it due to your other commitments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With this I conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Djurdjic. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Sir, I have a number of clarificatory questions arising from Defence counsel's cross-examination. This relates to your visit to Kosovo in March 1999. You were asked about the date on which you went to Kosovo during that period. Now, when the question was put to you, reference was made to a chronology of events by Defence counsel. I wonder if I could show you that chronology of events and perhaps that might assist you in remembering when it was you went to Kosovo in March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe Defence counsel was referring to P844, if we could have that up on the screen, please. And if we could go to page 6. If we could zoom in on that. I believe this page sets out the chronology of events from February onwards and also the early part of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you could glance at the document and let us know if this helps you remember when it was you made your visit to Kosovo in March 1999, before the war.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, this ends on my screen with the 5th of March, but it says clearly that I visited on the 2nd of March, visit of the chairman-in-office of review planning for the new mandate.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that your visit to Kosovo was on the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes -- well, it doesn't -- these dates don't go further than the 5th, so I don't know if it says anything about my visit later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We can go on to the next page if that helps you.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Since I'm not mentioned at all here, I suppose that the 2nd of March must have been my last visit before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And just to clarify, you gave some evidence on what you saw during your visit to Kosovo in March in relation to villages around Podujevo and civilians, et cetera. Did you view, observe, these incidents during this trip that we just spoke about, the one on the 2nd of March?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And am I correct that your subsequent visits to Kosovo in March were after the bombing?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, and they were not then in March, they were later on, because as you know the bombing started on the 24th of March. So I came back then after the war, and I must admit I don't know exactly when. It could have been in July.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Sir, I don't have any further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I mention for the transcript that perhaps in fairness to the memory of President Milosevic, page 79, line 1, a word "not" has been omitted. I think what was being said by the witness was: "If President Milosevic did not want an independent Kosovo ..." It would be problematic if we left the transcript uncorrected in that material matter. May I thank you, Ambassador, for your attendance once again, for the assistance that you have been able to give, and, of course, you may now return to your normal activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would thank counsel for their attention to time today. We continue on Monday with the videolink evidence that has been arranged. I think it's sitting in the afternoon, 2.15. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of July, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
